video_title: The Five Follies Investors Can’t Ignore | Protect the Pile Episode 23
gist: Four Hedgeye Asset Management PMs (Patrick 'RPK' Kent, Sam Ramen, David Salem, Brooks Cutrret) walk through Salem's 'five follies' essay — bombing Iran, disrespecting middle-power allies, a Fed chair pledging 2% inflation, assuming 'this time is different' in LLM competition, and hyperscaler capex — and translate each into positioning: a slow-boil rather than spike bid for oil and oilfield services, a resource-war/fragmentation theme (Hormuz tolls, Red Sea, Congo cobalt/copper), a bearish dollar with yen-intervention tail risk, and a view that AI is turning into low-differentiation cloud compute that compresses hyperscaler ROIC from 32%+ toward utility-like levels. The panel is broadly constructive on the tape (Quad 3-1-2-1 setup, S&P revenue +15% y/y, indices just off all-time highs) while flagging that the AI trade's return on invested capital, not its margins, is the thing that breaks.

insights.claim: David Salem applies historian Barbara Tuchman's three-part definition of folly — the policy had to be seen as foolish by fair-minded contemporaries, a feasible alternative had to exist, and it had to be a group's handiwork rather than one person's — as a screen for identifying policy and capital-allocation mistakes in real time.
insights.speaker: David Salem
insights.so_what: Gives investors a reusable three-question test to flag policies and corporate capex programs likely to be judged destructive in hindsight, before the market prices the mistake.
insights.quote: the policy that's being critiqued as a folly must have been perceived as foolish by fair-minded observers in its own day, in its own time

insights.claim: Salem's five current follies are: believing Iran can be bombed into compliance, 'messing with the middle powers' by disrespecting US allies, believing the Fed can control inflation on an ambiguous mandate, assuming 'this time is different' for large language model competition, and 'hyper hasty' hyperscaler spending whose payoff is unproven.
insights.speaker: David Salem
insights.so_what: Maps the panel's entire risk agenda — geopolitics, rates, and AI capex — into five discrete, monitorable failure modes.

insights.claim: Salem's general decision framework — rank-order your success metrics, specify the time horizon over which they are judged, then assign probabilities across the full range of plausible outcomes — is what he uses to conclude that current Iran and allied-nation policy fails on all three counts.
insights.speaker: David Salem
insights.so_what: The same three-question audit applied to a policy, a central bank pledge, or a corporate capex plan quickly exposes which ones have no defined success criteria and therefore no accountability.
insights.quote: folly is a renewable resource. There's never a shortage of folly around the world that one can critique

themes.theme: Iran, Hormuz Tolls and Energy Positioning

insights.claim: Sam Ramen prefers to buy energy equities after a Middle East 'deal' is finally announced and the headline risk resolves, rather than owning them into the ongoing weekend-to-weekend deal/no-deal whipsaw.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Argues for patience and a post-resolution entry in energy rather than chasing headline-driven spikes; the sell-off on 'deal' is the setup.
insights.quote: Just be the freaking deal in the straight of homes. Like have stuff happen. Let the stuff let energy some of these energy stocks sell off and then and then buy them.

insights.claim: Patrick Kent argues an oil spike to $150 would actually be bearish for energy equities beyond the very short term because it triggers demand-destruction fears that roll the stocks over quickly.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: Inverts the reflexive 'buy energy on conflict' trade — a vertical crude move is a signal to fade energy equities, not to add.
insights.quote: oil goes to 150 but you know what that's actually never that bullish for the energy stocks. It's good for like a little short time and then we start worrying about demand destruction and it rolls over very quickly

insights.claim: Kent expects an Iran–Oman arrangement that tightens international waters and imposes transit fees, permanently reducing tanker traffic below the prior 60–70 crossings per day and giving preference to Iranian oil flowing to China.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: A structurally lower, more expensive Hormuz throughput is a persistent cost tax on seaborne crude and a tailwind for tanker rates and freight-exposed names.
insights.quote: we're probably never going back to the 60 to 70, you know, tanker crossings a day that were there

insights.claim: Kent frames Houthi attacks in the Red Sea as the deliberate closing of the workaround route around Hormuz, producing a 'slow boil' under energy prices rather than a sharp spike — which he argues is the more compelling regime for owning energy names.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: A grinding, persistent premium sustains energy equity earnings far better than a spike-and-collapse; position for duration, not for the headline.
insights.quote: puts a slow boil under the price as opposed to um you know a sharper price increase

insights.claim: Oilfield services stocks rallied even though Halliburton and Schlumberger both fell on their reported results after flagging international business disruptions — implying a recovery and a longer earnings story if that disruption quiets down.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: Services names carry an embedded option on Middle East de-escalation that the post-earnings de-rating may not price.

insights.claim: Sam Ramen sees an unresolved internal Iranian power struggle — including reports on X of a harder-line faction pushing another religious revolution — as the reason for the on-again/off-again negotiation pattern, and warns Trump may return for 'vengeance' after the midterms having been publicly embarrassed by toll-based transit terms.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Frames the post-midterm window as a discrete re-escalation risk date for oil and defense exposure rather than a decaying-headline trade.
insights.quote: what I worry about is after the midterms, Trump goes back because, um, there's no way you cannot say that he just got embarrassed

insights.claim: Salem argues the US is reigniting a global war for resources, and that history — he cites Japan in the late 1930s and early 1940s — shows resource wars almost inevitably escalate into kinetic war, making reindustrialization plus secure access to talent and capital the necessary alternative.
insights.speaker: David Salem
insights.so_what: Supports a multi-year overweight to domestic industrial capacity and critical-minerals supply chains as a structural, not cyclical, theme.
insights.quote: Are we reigniting a war, a global war for resources, which history teaches us almost always inevitably leads to just kinetic war and a lot of bloodshed?

insights.claim: Kent reads the Congo's move to restrict cobalt and copper exports on the grounds that it doesn't extract enough value as another front in the same critical-minerals fight already underway in rare earths, not an isolated headline.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: Resource-holding nations moving up the value chain implies persistent input-cost inflation and supply risk for battery, EV, and electrification supply chains.

insights.claim: Brooks Cutrret argues warfare has been 'democratized' — drones, jet skis and entry-level equipment now let non-state actors create instability — so volatility in any extractable natural resource should be structurally higher and arrive from unpredictable vectors rather than from a traditional adversary.
insights.speaker: Brooks Cutrret
insights.so_what: Justifies a permanently higher volatility premium on commodities and shipping, and argues against models that assume state-actor-only disruption risk.
insights.quote: waging war used to be strictly something that was a nation state like oriented uh mover and and it's become democratized

insights.claim: Salem's third folly is the belief that the Fed can control inflation given an ambiguous mandate — he questions why the target is 2%, how it is measured, and over what horizon, noting no one says whether hitting it one month counts as victory if inflation is 5% the next quarter.
insights.speaker: David Salem
insights.so_what: If the mandate is unfalsifiable, Fed guidance carries less information than markets price, arguing for lower confidence in forward-rate paths anchored on target credibility.

insights.claim: Salem says the new Fed chair's flat promise 'we will get to 2%' would be an illegal promissory statement if made by an asset manager about returns, and that the failure to instead tell Congress the mandate is not actionable reflects a lack of intellectual integrity rather than a lack of brainpower.
insights.speaker: David Salem
insights.so_what: A chair over-promising on an unachievable target sets up a credibility break that would be repriced first in the long end and in inflation breakevens.
insights.quote: We would never say I will deliver a 14% return and a you know blank sharp ratio.

insights.claim: Sam Ramen believes the Fed chair should have hiked at the last meeting to establish credibility and set the tone for the year, and thinks bond yields would likely have fallen on that decision rather than risen.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: A hawkish surprise being bond-bullish is the non-consensus reaction function; it implies the long end is trading on credibility, not on the policy rate itself.
insights.quote: I would not be surprised if bond yields had gone down on that decision

insights.claim: Housing-related equities had started to break out and are now breaking down again as mortgage rates back up, putting them back on the panel's watch list.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Housing equities are the cleanest real-time read on whether the long end is cooperating; their failed breakout is an early warning on the rate path.
insights.quote: they were starting to break out and now they're all breaking down because the mortgage rates back

themes.theme: Yen Intervention, Carry Trade and the Japan Bargain

insights.claim: Sam Ramen frames the Treasury's yen problem structurally: Japan is the largest owner of US Treasuries, so as Japanese bond yields rise it becomes compelling for Japanese capital to repatriate and buy domestic bonds instead of dollar-hedged Treasuries — which is precisely what US officials are trying to prevent by intervening.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Makes Japanese domestic yields a leading indicator for US long-end demand; a JGB yield rise is a direct bid-side risk to Treasuries.
insights.quote: Japan owns it's the largest owner of US treasuries

insights.claim: With speculative yen shorts at record levels on one side and the US Treasury's balance sheet on the other, Ramen expects the market to keep testing officials on how much balance sheet they will commit — a left-field risk that blindsides equity investors.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Record one-sided positioning plus an official counterparty is the classic setup for a violent unwind; size equity risk with that tail in mind.
insights.quote: the short position in the yen is is like a record levels

insights.claim: Salem says he cannot identify the success metrics, time horizon, or considered outcome range behind Bessent using US resources to strengthen the yen and weaken the dollar, and calls the policy 'too clever by half'; on intervention generally, he says it has only ever 'worked' on a 48-hour horizon, never durably.
insights.speaker: David Salem
insights.so_what: Treat any yen-strengthening intervention as a fade beyond a two-day window unless explicit, measurable objectives are published.
insights.quote: what do you mean really works? It never works

insights.claim: Kent warns that intervening to strengthen the yen against a record short position with the carry trade still on could catalyze an unanticipated unwind, noting that two summers ago the carry trade had migrated into large-cap tech and may now sit in Korean DRAM and other 'moonshot' stocks.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific transmission channel — a yen squeeze hits the most crowded momentum equities first, not the currency market.

insights.claim: Salem's intuition is that the administration is carving Japan out from the broader allied-pressure campaign because the US depends on Japan for shipbuilding and ship maintenance and because the 'missile map' — which Trump himself let slip — is heavily in Iran's favor, leaving the US short of munitions.
insights.speaker: David Salem
insights.so_what: Explains the yen policy as military-industrial dependence rather than FX management, and points to Japanese shipbuilding and US munitions capacity as the beneficiaries.
insights.quote: the missile map is very very heavily in Iran's favor

themes.theme: Open vs Closed Weights and the Token Margin Pool

insights.claim: Sam Ramen expects an 80/20 split where most query volume is served cheaply by open-source models while the heavy frontier and coding workloads go to frontier labs — meaning roughly 10–20% of usage carries most of the margin.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Frames token volume growth as a poor proxy for AI profit growth; the profit pool concentrates in a narrow slice of high-end workloads.
insights.quote: most of the volume is in the is in the cheap cheaper models and then uh you know the 10% 20% whatever the number is is going to be with the frontier labs where where the most of the margin is going to be

insights.claim: Ramen argues the Chinese models' cost advantage was 'smoke and mirrors' — cheaper on paper, but as expensive or more expensive than US models in actual cost to produce a delivered token.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Undercuts the bear case that Chinese models structurally deflate frontier-model pricing, and shifts the competitive threat to US-based open-source alternatives.
insights.quote: what we discovered with the Chinese model is that it was all a got a smoke and mirrors

insights.claim: Ramen expects US-based open-source models to become the foundation layer sitting beneath a hyperscaler orchestration layer at AWS, Azure and GCP, where enterprises set a budget and let the platform route queries across models to optimize spend.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Positions the model-agnostic hyperscalers, not any individual model provider, as the durable toll collector on enterprise AI spend.

insights.claim: Kent counters that if models commoditize and compete away pricing, AI stops being a premium closed-model business and becomes just continued growth in ordinary cloud compute — evolutionary rather than revolutionary — noting Microsoft's disclosure that the bulk of its AI revenue traces back to loss-making OpenAI.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: If AI is just a cloud migration extension, it deserves cloud multiples and cloud growth rates rather than a separate AI re-rating.

themes.theme: Hyperscaler Capex, ROIC Compression and Cost of Capital

insights.claim: Kent flags that Google raised capex guidance and disclosed multi-year obligations, then followed a recent share offering with another debt deal, while Oracle's CDS keeps pushing higher — at 200 basis points not yet alarming but well above the last few years.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: Oracle CDS at 200bps is a concrete, trackable early-warning gauge on AI-capex credit stress; watch it alongside each new hyperscaler debt issue.
insights.quote: Oracle CDS is continues to just be pushing higher. Now it's not alarming at 200 basis points but it's up a lot from where it was over the last few years

insights.claim: Kent's core bear case is that AI capex intensity mechanically lowers hyperscaler return on invested capital — a 32%-plus ROIC business heading toward something between historical hyperscaler returns and the roughly 4% ROIC of utilities — regardless of how good reported margins look.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: Says to value hyperscalers on ROIC trajectory rather than operating margin; falling incremental returns compress the multiple even with growing profits.
insights.quote: this business is on its way to being something between what hyperscalers were and the 4% ROIC that is utilities

insights.claim: Ramen's counter is that hyperscalers are currently under-earning on the new AI business because all the capex is being digested up front while the enterprise contracts behind it are three-to-five-year — closer to five-year — streams of contractual ARR that have yet to roll through the P&L.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Provides the bull rebuttal with a testable timeline: if contracted ARR does not visibly convert over the next several years, the ROIC bear case wins.
insights.quote: the hyperscalers are under earning on the incremental business

insights.claim: Ramen calls the Microsoft and Amazon earnings calls the two most important prints of the season for the AI debate because they resolved whether the hyperscalers are actually making money on the investment, citing Andy Jassy's walkthrough of how power-shell versus server spend is layered in and roughly 37–38% operating margins on Amazon's overall business.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Points to specific disclosures investors can re-read for the timing of capex recognition, and identifies a pivot point where money began rotating within the AI complex.
insights.quote: those two calls Microsoft oft and Amazon were probably two of the most important calls coming out of earnings

insights.claim: Ramen argues Meta is a structurally different stock from the other hyperscalers because winning enterprise cloud contracts requires an enterprise salesforce, security and support that took GCP years to build — so Meta and SpaceX will capture swing capacity and startup demand, not multi-year enterprise contracts.
insights.speaker: Sam Ramen
insights.so_what: Separates credible enterprise cloud competitors from compute-rich entrants; do not underwrite Meta or SpaceX compute as a near-term share threat to AWS or Azure.
insights.quote: Meta if they want to do that they want to play in that game there's a ways to go which is why I think Meta is a different animal in terms of the stock than these other ones

insights.claim: Kent draws an explicit analogy to the CDN business, where the multiple compressed and stayed low for years because growth was fine but pricing turned negative once telecom incumbents competed the business away — while Ramen pushes back that hyperscalers differ because of the software application layer above the compute.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: Supplies a historical template for how a fast-growing infrastructure business can de-rate for years on price, not volume — the specific risk to watch in cloud AI.
insights.quote: that multiple compressed and then stayed low for a long time because the growth was fine but the pricing actually was negative

insights.claim: Brooks Cutrret argues AI compute is heading toward a glut and could eventually be monetized through a futures-style market for compute — his old fund pitched H100-level GPU tranche futures — while noting only about 2.2% of households subscribe to an AI or LLM provider, so mass adoption at 60–80% penetration would require far cheaper, free, or ad-supported delivery.
insights.speaker: Brooks Cutrret
insights.so_what: The 2.2% household penetration figure sets the scale of price deflation required for consumer AI to scale, and compute futures would mark the point at which capacity becomes a traded commodity.
insights.quote: It's like 2.2% of households have subscribed to a an AI or like an LLM provider

insights.claim: Salem reduces follies four and five to a single corporate-finance question — what is your cost of capital, and will the project's return exceed it — and warns that as hyperscalers layer on major dollops of debt, both the shareholder base and the cost of equity capital change, raising the blended cost of capital rather than lowering it.
insights.speaker: David Salem
insights.so_what: The overlooked variable in the AI capex debate: debt-funded buildouts raise the equity cost of capital, so the hurdle rate rises exactly as incremental returns fall.
insights.quote: as we layer on more and more and more debt, not only does the shareholder base that we're attracting or repelling morph, evolve and change, but so do does our cost of equity capital

insights.claim: Kent argues cyber security stocks are acting well for good reason because the agentic layer has only just been unleashed and is already producing a steady stream of disclosed breaches, implying far more incidents than are publicly known.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: Positions cyber security as the derivative long on AI agent deployment, with a demand driver independent of whether AI capex returns clear their cost of capital.
insights.quote: cyber cyber stocks been acting well. They should be because we've just unleashed the agentic layer like recently

insights.claim: Hedgeye's monthly quad setup for the US is 3-1-2-1, which Salem and Kent characterize as a bullish environment, with equities just off all-time highs as of Friday August 7.
insights.speaker: David Salem
insights.so_what: Defines the house macro regime the rest of the discussion's bearish structural views must be traded against — constructive near term, structurally cautious.
insights.quote: 312 of the monthly uh qu setups for the US, although we do track 50 other national economies

insights.claim: S&P 500 revenue is running roughly 15% year-over-year, which Kent notes creates a heavy comparison hurdle for 2027, while only about 2% of the index reports next week and the retail names — the next real consumer read — are still a few weeks out.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: Flags a specific forward risk: 2027 comps against 15% revenue growth are the setup for a growth-rate-of-change disappointment even if absolute results hold.

insights.claim: Kent's liquidity measures read neutral rather than bullish, so he attributes the recent breakout partly to re-leveraging, and warns that margin borrowing and leverage trading make the violence of directional moves harder to anticipate even with liquidity indicators.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: A leverage-driven breakout on neutral liquidity means downside gaps can be far larger than the liquidity signal implies; size accordingly.

insights.claim: Hedgeye has recently turned bearish the dollar after it broke trend, and Kent ties that view to the fragmenting multipolar world and escalating resource fights.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), host
insights.so_what: A house bearish-dollar signal that reinforces the commodity, gold-adjacent and international-equity side of the resource-fragmentation trade.
insights.quote: we've recently kind of now gone bearish the dollar uh as we broke you know broke trend
